solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Raise fewer arguments after convincing demonstration

parts.note: to raise an objection is to object
less = fewer
on = after, later

explanation.surface: Someone learns to stop quibbling after being shown something that settles the argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raise' is a verb about objections, not lifting; 'after' does double duty, meaning 'on' and placing that piece last.
explanation.definitionFit: An object lesson is a practical example that convincingly demonstrates a principle.

clue.text: Keep returning unwrapped porcelain box

indicators.note: going back the way it came: the letters are read in reverse
the wrapping, the outer letters, comes off

parts.note: Sèvres porcelain, made at the French factory
used literally

explanation.surface: A collector keeps sending back a piece of china that arrived without its packing.
explanation.walkthrough: SEVRES and BOX run together as SEVRESBOX; unwrapping strips the outer S and X to leave EVRESBO, which reads OBSERVE backwards. 'Keep' is the verb, as in keeping or observing a rule.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of complying: you keep the Sabbath or a rule in the same way you observe it.

clue.text: American Lord is mocking physical exercise drills

parts.note: he jeers = he is mocking
PE = physical education, school exercise

explanation.surface: An American aristocrat sneers at a keep-fit regime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lord' is the exclamation, as in 'Lord!', and 'Jeepers!' is its American equivalent. 'Drills' looks like a noun for the exercises; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeepers is a mild American exclamation of surprise, like 'Lord!'.

clue.text: Disc that fastens to cycle snatched by phoney cleaner

indicators.note: the letters go round: BU moves from the front to the back

parts.note: cod = sham, mock
a BUTTON, cycled so BU goes to the end

explanation.surface: A fake cleaner has pinched a disc that fixes onto a bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycle' reads as a bicycle in the surface; here it is an instruction to rotate BUTTON. COD for fake is a British usage, as in cod science.
explanation.definitionFit: A cotton bud is a swab on a stick for cleaning ears and other small spaces.

clue.text: See promotional material a lot

parts.note: lo = see, behold
advertisements

explanation.surface: Someone is told they will see a great deal of advertising.
explanation.walkthrough: LO is the old word for 'see!' or 'behold', a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal British plural used as a quantity word, as in 'loads of time'.

clue.text: Matter this woman put on report

parts.note: the pronoun for a woman
the report of a gun is its bang

explanation.surface: An issue a particular woman has raised in her report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' is a document in the surface and a loud noise in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A shebang is an affair or matter, as in 'the whole shebang'.

clue.text: By 8 o'clock, let up cast to replace player

indicators.note: to replace means the player is taken out of o'clock, with the other letters going in its stead

parts.note: a lock is a forward player in rugby

indicators.note: cast means the letters of let up are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: By eight in the evening, a cast member eases off and an understudy goes on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' looks like the stage actor of the surface, but it is the rugby lock, a second-row forward; '8' in the definition means multiplied by eight.
explanation.definitionFit: Octuple means eightfold, so something octuple has been multiplied by eight.

clue.text: It'll deflect water if turned off, so it's said

indicators.note: so it's said tells us the answer sounds like these words spoken aloud

parts.note: if gives WHETHER; if can mean whether, and turned off means bored; said together they sound like the answer

explanation.surface: Something that keeps water away, assuming it has been switched off, or so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned off' looks like switched off but means bored. WHETHER plus BORED, said aloud, gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A weatherboard is a sloping board fixed to the bottom of a door or a wall to throw off rain.

clue.text: Most like a picnic meal, the rest of the afternoon free of shackles

indicators.note: shackles bind both ends, so being free of them means losing the first and last letters

parts.words: meal, the rest of the afternoon
parts.note: tea is an afternoon meal, and a siesta is the afternoon's rest or nap; together they run on as one string

explanation.surface: A meal most like a picnic, with the afternoon spent lazing about without restraint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a picnic' means something easy, as in 'no picnic'. TEASIESTA loses its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something called a picnic is easy; the superlative means the least difficult of all.

clue.text: A doubter, but not one initially coming clean

indicators.note: but not one means a single letter is taken away from the word for doubter

parts.note: a sceptic doubts things

indicators.note: initially means only the first letter of coming is used

explanation.surface: A sceptic refuses to come clean about anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming clean' reads as one phrase, but 'clean' is the definition and 'coming' only lends its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Aseptic means free from germs that cause infection, so sterile or clean.

clue.text: On set of shelves put something one may have to bear weight of TV

indicators.note: in a down clue, the burden goes on top of the shelves
places the first piece in that position

parts.words: something one may have to bear weight of
parts.note: a cross to bear is a burden
a dresser is a kitchen cabinet with shelves

explanation.surface: Instructions for standing a heavy television on a shelf unit.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about a heavy television set; TV is the abbreviation for transvestite.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbreviation: TV stands for transvestite, someone who wears the clothes of the other sex.

clue.text: Ring HQ about confiscating Resistance weapon

indicators.note: confiscating means taking and holding, so the reversed word holds the letter
about means turned round, so the base word is read backwards

parts.note: a depot is a headquarters or base
R is the physics symbol for resistance
a ring is O-shaped

explanation.surface: Ring headquarters about the seizing of a weapon from the Resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: DEPOT reversed gives TOPED, which takes in R; O, the ring, goes on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A torpedo is a self-propelled underwater missile fired at ships.

clue.text: Imposter dropping soft soap?

parts.note: a sham is a fraud or impostor
a dropping, as from a dog

explanation.surface: A fraud who gives up flattering people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dropping soft soap' reads as giving up flattery; 'soft soap' is really the liquid kind, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Shampoo is a soft, liquid soap, the question mark flagging the literal reading of an idiom.

clue.text: Real Madrid and Barcelona? Not for them the 1-1?

indicators.note: these teams go without the word 'the', so it is removed

parts.note: two football teams, two elevens
el is 'the' in Spanish, fitting for Spanish clubs

explanation.surface: A pundit says the two Spanish giants are never content with a draw.
explanation.walkthrough: '1-1' looks like a scoreline; it is betting odds. The Spanish 'the' comes out of ELEVENS because the teams are Spanish.
explanation.definitionFit: Bookmakers' language: a bet at 1-1 wins as much as the stake, and the British call those odds evens.

clue.text: Gradually categorising Burns this way?

definitions.meaning: burns are classed as first, second or third degree

explanation.surface: Someone works slowly through the poems of Robert Burns, sorting them.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital B makes Burns the Scottish poet; here they are injuries, classed as first-, second- or third-degree.
explanation.definitionFit: By degrees means gradually, one step at a time.

clue.text: In doldrums after losing house, have to come out

indicators.note: the second piece goes inside the first

parts.note: DOLDRUMS without DRUM

indicators.note: the doldrums once they have lost the house

parts.note: drum is British slang for a house or flat
own = have, plus TO

explanation.surface: A struggling worker who has lost their home has to move out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come out' is British for going on strike, and 'have' is 'own', not a helping verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To down tools is to stop work, to come out on strike.

clue.text: Light during day charges pointer?

indicators.note: charges means the first pieces rush into the dog's name

parts.note: a pointer is a breed of dog, and bow-wow is a nursery word for a dog; the question mark flags the example
during means in

explanation.surface: A dog charges about in daylight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' looks like daylight, but in architecture a light is a window or one pane of it.
explanation.definitionFit: In architecture a light is a window, and a bow window is one curving outwards.

clue.text: Conflicts wear out nurses very much

indicators.note: nurses means the rearranged letters hold the other piece as if cradling it
out means the letters of wear are knocked into a new order

parts.note: far, as in far better, means very much

explanation.surface: Endless conflicts wear out the nurses badly.
explanation.walkthrough: WARE, an anagram of wear, holds FAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Warfare is armed fighting between groups, a collective word for conflicts.

clue.text: Left abandoned, one naturally sticks with Trump's state force

parts.note: a limpet clings to rocks
L = left, removed
Trump presides over the US

explanation.surface: A politician on the left sticks with the president's forces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a political side, but it is just the letter to drop. 'State' is the whole country, not one of the fifty.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from physics: impetus is the momentum or driving force that keeps something moving.

clue.text: Who dispatches present?

definitions.meaning: one who offs, that is kills

explanation.surface: A question about who sends out a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: To off someone is slang for to kill them, so an offer is one who dispatches; 'dispatches' looks like posting a parcel.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the verb, to hold something out for acceptance, and a jokey noun, one who offs, or kills.

clue.text: Busy, having to cancel opening, say: "May I?"

indicators.note: to cancel the opening means dropping the first letter of the month word

parts.note: May is an example of a month, which is what say signals
the ego is the I, the self

explanation.surface: A busy person, having to call off a launch, asks politely for permission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May I?' looks like a polite request. Really May is a month (MONTH, minus its first letter) and I is EGO.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on the go is constantly active and busy.

clue.text: Perhaps Leeuwarder is enthralled by the Rev. Paisley?

parts.note: Fr = Father, a title for a clergyman
the Rev. Ian Paisley, Northern Irish preacher and politician
used literally

explanation.surface: A man from a Dutch city is spellbound by the Northern Irish preacher Ian Paisley.
explanation.walkthrough: Leeuwarden is the capital of Friesland in the Netherlands, so someone from there is an example of a Frisian.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Leeuwarden, the Frisian capital, is a Frisian.

clue.text: Suitable support found in Apple's first operating system

indicators.note: found in means the support piece sits inside the others
first means only the opening letter of Apple's is used

parts.note: OS is the computing abbreviation for operating system
a prop supports something

explanation.surface: A tech reviewer finds a fitting feature in an early Apple operating system.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an Apple product, but only its initial letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Apropos means relevant or fitting to the matter in hand, so appropriate.

clue.text: Very fine cut on the ear

indicators.note: as it strikes the ear, heard not seen

parts.note: to shear is to cut

explanation.surface: A very neat haircut round the ear.
explanation.walkthrough: The haircut picture makes 'on the ear' look like where the cut is.
explanation.definitionFit: A textile sense: sheer describes gauzy cloth so fine it is see-through.

clue.text: Some juicy gossip gripped parting garden visitors

parts.note: tits are small garden birds
bit = gripped with the teeth

explanation.surface: Delicious rumours seized upon as the garden guests say goodbye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gripped' looks like the container word, but it is BIT; 'parting' does the containing.
explanation.definitionFit: Titbits are small tasty morsels of news or gossip.

clue.text: Recruit Don's neighbour to guard large amount

parts.note: the rivers Don and Dee flow into the sea side by side at Aberdeen
a raft of = a large number of

explanation.surface: A new soldier is posted next to a university don to protect a large sum.
explanation.walkthrough: Don is a Scottish river, not a lecturer or a Mafia boss.
explanation.definitionFit: American usage: the draft is conscription, so a draftee is a recruit called up by it.

clue.text: Indicate corruption of old Commonwealth realm

parts.note: O = old
Belize keeps the British monarch as head of state

explanation.surface: Pointing to graft in a former Commonwealth country.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is political corruption; the definition is textual, marking a passage in a manuscript as corrupt.
explanation.definitionFit: To obelize is to mark a word or passage with an obelus as spurious or corrupt.

clue.text: I will not work for retiring food transporter

indicators.note: going back: the whole string is read in reverse

parts.note: the refusal
op = opus, a work
in print 'I will not work' is set in italics: stressed

explanation.surface: A striker's slogan: I won't work for anyone who is stepping down.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue italicises 'I will not work', so the words are STRESSED; NO OP STRESSED read backwards is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A dessertspoon carries pudding to the mouth.
